title: SMT solver models as counterexamples
description: When Z3 says SAT to the negated property, its model is a concrete counterexample: variable assignments that violate the claim. Reading the model — mapping solver variables back to program state — turns 'property false' into 'here, with these inputs, it breaks'.
method: Negate the property; ask the solver; on SAT, extract the model; map back to program inputs; present as a failing case.
usage: Always extract and concretize the model; a counterexample you can't replay is just a rumor.

demo.code:
print('property: x > 0 implies f(x) > 0')
print('solver model: x = -3 -> f(-3) = 5? no: f(-3) = -1')
print('counterexample: x=-3 violates the claim')

title: Alloy instance generation
description: Alloy's analyzer doesn't just say 'no' — it shows a concrete instance violating the assertion, rendered as a diagram. Counterexamples as pictures: the design flaw is visible, not just logical. It's the most humane counterexample generator in formal methods.
method: Write the model and assertion; the analyzer produces a counterexample instance within scope; visualize and inspect.
usage: Inspect counterexamples visually; they're design feedback, not just failures.

demo.code:
print('assertion: no orphaned files')
print('counterexample: [File F1] --no owner--> (diagram shown)')
print('design fix: require owner on creation')

title: Adversarial example generation (ML)
description: For ML models, counterexamples are adversarial inputs: tiny perturbations flipping the prediction. Generators (FGSM, PGD) systematically find them, and each one refutes the claim 'the model is robust here'. Adversarial counterexamples drove the entire robustness research program.
method: Gradient-guided perturbation within an epsilon ball; verify the prediction flips; the perturbed input is the counterexample.
usage: Generate adversarially during training (adversarial training); test robustness on held-out attacks.

demo.code:
print('image classified "panda" (99%); PGD epsilon=0.03 -> "gibbon" (87%)')
print('counterexample: imperceptible perturbation flips prediction')

title: Counterexample explanation
description: A raw counterexample ('x=-3') isn't an explanation. Explanation layers map the counterexample to the design decision it refutes, highlight the relevant code path, and suggest the fix shape. The generator's job isn't done when it finds the break — it's done when a human understands it.
method: Map the counterexample to code paths; identify the refuted assumption; generate the explanation with fix suggestions.
usage: Invest in explanation; a counterexample nobody understands is a counterexample wasted.

demo.code:
print('counterexample: x=-3')
print('explanation: abs() assumed non-negative input (line 12); x=-3 refutes it')
print('suggested fix: handle negatives or strengthen precondition')

title: Witness generation for liveness
description: Liveness violations ('something good eventually happens') need infinite counterexamples — lassos (a stem plus a cycle avoiding the good thing). Generators produce the lasso: the finite representation of 'never'. It's the counterexample shape for progress properties.
method: Search for lassos avoiding the desired state; the (stem, cycle) pair is the violation; present it as 'repeats forever without progress'.
usage: Read liveness counterexamples as 'this cycle repeats forever'; the fix breaks the cycle.

demo.code:
print('liveness: every request eventually granted')
print('lasso: request -> retry -> request -> retry ... (grant never occurs)')

title: Counterexample databases
description: Counterexamples are assets: a database of past counterexamples (with the bug, the fix, and the regression test) turns one team's found bug into every team's avoided bug. New code is checked against the historical counterexample corpus automatically.
method: Archive (counterexample, bug, fix, test); check new code against the corpus; the corpus grows with every found bug.
usage: Archive every significant counterexample; make the corpus check part of CI.

demo.code:
print('corpus: 1,204 counterexamples archived')
print('new parser checked vs corpus: 3 historical patterns matched -> flagged pre-merge')

title: Mutation-driven counterexamples
description: Mutate the program slightly and check whether the property still holds: surviving mutants are counterexamples to the claim 'the tests verify the property'. Each surviving mutant is a concrete program variant your verification misses — a gap made tangible.
method: Generate mutants; check the property per mutant; survivors are verification gaps; strengthen the property or tests.
usage: Treat surviving mutants as counterexamples to your verification, not just your tests.

demo.code:
print('mutant: > changed to >= in bounds check')
print('property still "holds" -> SURVIVED: verification gap (off-by-one not caught)')

title: TLC minimal traces
description: TLC reports the shortest trace to a violation — the minimal sequence of states from init to bug. Minimal traces are debuggable traces: every step matters, and the design flaw is usually obvious at the step where the invariant first breaks.
method: Model check; on violation, extract the minimal trace; walk it step by step; find where the design went wrong.
usage: Walk the trace from the start; the bug is at the first surprising step.

demo.code:
print('TLC: invariant violated at state 7 of 7-step trace')
print('step 4: second leader elected -> design flaw: election not fenced')
